processing: Ripe pu-erh from a numbered Xiaguan recipe: wet-piled leaf steamed and pressed into a cake. A tighter iron-pressed version is sold as T8663.
harvest_season: No fixed picking is advertised; as a recipe tea it is defined by the blend and the production year.
appearance_dry: A firmly pressed, dark reddish-brown cake, sold in 357 g for the Jin Bang version.
appearance_liquor: Dark red-brown and clear, as is typical of ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Dark brown leaf and fragments, soft after steeping.
taste_profile: As is typical of ripe pu-erh, expect an earthy, woody body with smooth sweetness; individual years can differ with age and storage.

brewing.notes: Xiaguan pressings can be hard, the iron-pressed T version especially: use a pick, chip along the edge and rinse twice before the first cup.

vintage_note: Sold by production year, usually as a cake of a few hundred grams, with versions such as a 2013 T8663 and a 2018 Jin Bang on the market. As with most factory shu, it is drunk young or after several years of rest. Check whether the wrapper says 8663 or T8663, since the second is pressed much harder.
description:
8663 is a recipe number from the Xiaguan tea factory in Dali, known for tuos and for firm pressing. It is a factory shu of the old-fashioned kind: you buy a code and a year, not a mountain or a story.

The code itself tells you something. The 86 is read as the year of the recipe, 1986, and the final 3 marks Xiaguan as the factory. The digit in the middle relates to the material, but accounts of its exact meaning disagree, so do not read too much into it.

Expect the usual pleasures of ripe pu-erh: dark, woody and smooth. Xiaguan cakes reward a little patience, as a hard pressing opens slowly. Rinse well and give a young cake some air if it smells of the pile.

For buyers the key distinction is plain 8663 against T8663, the tighter iron cake. Jin Bang is the series name on some recent wrappers. Fakes are a known issue with popular Xiaguan teas, so buy from a seller you trust.
history:
The number points to a recipe dating to 1986, according to retailers' reading of the code; a factory document confirming it has not been traced. The Xiaguan factory itself dates to 1941, and the tea is one of many numbered recipes from it.

Xiaguan launched its Jin Bang series in 2014, and 8663 became one of its better-known members.
